title: Bosch Digital Design System (BDDS) - Foundational Research

scope.purpose: Transform the foundational research findings about the Bosch Digital Design System into an AI-readable JSON structure.
covered_topics: Practical implications for designers, developers, and product teams
excluded_topics: Official AI rules not confirmed by Bosch sources

executive_summary.short_definition: The Bosch Digital Design System (BDDS) is the official standardized digital design and development system for Bosch digital touchpoints. It extends the Bosch Brand Guide into digital products by providing shared guidelines, reusable design assets, implementation components, accessibility rules, and governance mechanisms.
executive_summary.main_conclusion: BDDS should be understood as an ecosystem rather than a single guideline page. The ecosystem connects the Bosch Brand Guide, BDDS documentation, Bosch UI Kit in Figma, Frontend Kit (FROK), Digital Offer Consent Kit (DOCK), Brand Platform (Frontify), Figma, design tokens, accessibility standards, and update/migration processes.
practical_reading: For Bosch-branded digital products, BDDS is the expected default standard.
BDDS exists to ensure consistent, accessible, high-quality, and brand-compliant digital experiences.
The system reduces fragmentation by giving designers, developers, and product teams a shared language and reusable foundation.
The system is increasingly token-driven, especially through Digital Color System 2.
Accessibility is embedded into the design system and should not be treated as an optional add-on.

bdds_definition.statement: BDDS is Bosch's official design system for digital products and touchpoints.
bdds_definition.expanded_definition: BDDS combines digital design guidelines, reusable design assets, frontend implementation components, accessibility standards, governance processes, and documentation into one system. It enables Bosch business units and product teams to design, develop, and operate digital interfaces using a shared language, shared tools, and predefined resources.

relationship_to_bosch_brand_guide.statement: BDDS is the digital extension and supplement of the Bosch Brand Guide.
implications: BDDS is not a parallel visual language.
BDDS does not replace the Bosch Brand Guide.
BDDS operationalizes Bosch brand principles for digital interfaces.
When there is uncertainty, Bosch Brand Guide plus BDDS documentation should be treated as the root authority.

mandatory_usage.status: Binding for Bosch products, according to the referenced internal BDDS documentation and central directive framing.
mandatory_usage.rule_of_thumb: Bosch-branded digital products should default to BDDS unless a justified exception applies.
exceptions_or_case_by_case_contexts: Third-party software with its own style guide
Hybrid contexts where another brand or platform style guide must be evaluated
Special project contexts that require formal design governance discussion
team_implications: Teams should not create custom UI styles when BDDS patterns already exist.
Teams should reuse official components as defined.
Teams should stay aligned with BDDS updates.
Design and development should use the same system logic.
Product teams should treat divergence from BDDS as an exception requiring justification.

ecosystem.statement: BDDS functions as a multi-part ecosystem connecting corporate design, documentation, design libraries, implementation libraries, compliance assets, and operational support.

components.name: Bosch Brand Guide

components.relationship_to_bdds: BDDS extends the Brand Guide into digital touchpoints.

components.name: BDDS Documentation

components.name: Bosch UI Kit

components.name: Frontend Kit (FROK)
components.role: Provides reusable frontend components, styles, typography, icons, and implementation-ready assets for web projects based on BDDS.
components.relationship_to_bdds: Serves as the web development implementation layer of BDDS.

components.name: Digital Offer Consent Kit (DOCK)
components.role: Supports consent-related digital experiences and compliance needs, such as consent and cookie-related flows.
components.relationship_to_bdds: Part of the BDDS ecosystem alongside FROK and Bosch UI Kit.

components.name: Brand Platform (Frontify)
components.role: Documents, facilitates, and streamlines branding, marketing, and development operations. Provides access to guidelines and brand assets.
components.relationship_to_bdds: Operational documentation and asset management layer for Bosch brand and BDDS materials.

components.name: Figma
components.role: Cloud-based collaborative design and prototyping tool connected to official Bosch UI libraries and regular updates.
components.relationship_to_bdds: Main design workspace for applying BDDS through official libraries and components.

components.name: Papirfly / Layout Creator

components.relationship_to_bdds: Adjacent brand-compliant asset generation tool within the broader Bosch design and brand ecosystem.

components.name: Design Tokens
components.role: Provide structured, reusable, tool-agnostic definitions for foundational design decisions such as colors and, in future expansion, additional foundations like typography, spacing, interface formats, and themes.
components.relationship_to_bdds: Bridge design and code by turning design foundations into synchronized variables.

core_principles.meaning: Bosch digital products should share recognizable visual and interaction patterns across products and platforms.
core_principles.why_it_matters: Consistent usage of BDDS creates high recognition value and strengthens trust in the Bosch brand.

core_principles.meaning: Standard BDDS components should be used as defined whenever possible.
core_principles.why_it_matters: Reusing standard components reduces rework, avoids fragmentation, and preserves system-level quality.

core_principles.meaning: Accessibility requirements should be embedded in components, colors, typography, interaction states, and content rules.
core_principles.why_it_matters: This helps Bosch teams meet usability, inclusion, and legal requirements without treating accessibility as a late-stage patch.

core_principles.meaning: Design assets and implementation components should follow the same system logic.
core_principles.why_it_matters: Alignment between Figma libraries and FROK reduces drift between design intent and production implementation.

core_principles.meaning: The system must support adoption across many teams, products, touchpoints, and business units.
core_principles.why_it_matters: Bosch operates globally, so local custom design solutions must be minimized in favor of scalable shared standards.

core_principles.meaning: Teams should plan for regular library, component, and token updates.
core_principles.why_it_matters: Continuous updates prevent design system drift, outdated components, and accessibility or compliance gaps.

core_principles.meaning: BDDS defines boundaries while enabling teams to work independently inside those boundaries.
core_principles.why_it_matters: This balances central brand governance with decentralized product team execution.

quality.description: Centralized templates and standardized components increase the quality of digital interfaces.

speed.description: Reusable assets accelerate releases and reduce project time.

usability.description: Self-similar interaction patterns across Bosch applications promote trust and secure interaction.

brand_protection.description: Reusing provided design and interaction elements protects Bosch's global brand identity.

design_foundations.overview: BDDS foundations define the recurring visual and interaction basics used across digital products. These include typography, layout, spacing, colors, icons, components, states, and accessibility rules.

typography.summary: Typography is inherited from Bosch corporate design and adapted for digital readability and accessibility.
known_findings: Typography guidance is part of BDDS updates.
Readable text sizing and scalable units are important for accessibility.
The corporate typeface and consistent text hierarchy support legibility and brand consistency.
typography.ai_interpretation: AI-generated Bosch digital interfaces should avoid arbitrary fonts and should preserve Bosch typography hierarchy, readability, and spacing discipline.

layout_and_grid.summary: Layout and grid rules provide spatial consistency across responsive digital products.
known_findings: BDDS includes digital touchpoint and foundation documentation.
Designs should use structured layouts and reusable patterns rather than ad-hoc composition.
Layout decisions should support accessibility, responsive behavior, and clear hierarchy.
layout_and_grid.ai_interpretation: AI-generated interfaces should use clean hierarchy, consistent spacing, predictable alignment, and responsive structure instead of decorative or inconsistent layouts.

spacing.summary: Spacing is a foundational design dimension that supports readability, visual rhythm, and consistent component composition.
known_findings: Spacing should be treated as a systematic foundation rather than arbitrary white space.
Future token expansion is expected to include foundational tokens beyond color.
spacing.ai_interpretation: AI-generated layouts should avoid dense, inconsistent spacing and should use systematic margins, padding, and separation between components.

color.summary: Color is governed through the Bosch Digital Color System 2, which uses design tokens and accessibility-oriented combinations.
known_findings: The update affects the entire BDDS landscape, including Bosch UI Kit Figma libraries and FROK.
The color system is tool- and framework-agnostic.
The system enables theming, multibrand capability, and accessibility by default.

digital_color_system_2.status: Rolled out across the Bosch Digital Design System according to the Q2 2025 UI Roundtable materials.
digital_color_system_2.strategic_meaning: Digital Color System 2 is not only a color palette update. It is a system architecture update that makes color usage more modular, tokenized, scalable, and accessible.

key_features.meaning: Color definitions are stored as reusable, machine-readable tokens.
Color tokens can be consumed across different design tools and development frameworks.
Individual brand color configurations can be supported on request.
Attributes and naming are optimized for modularity.
Color-scheme names were simplified to be more intuitive.
Consistent color usage is supported across schemes and components.
New schemes and nested color logic create additional design possibilities.
Disabled state colors were unified across schemes.
Each palette now includes white and black by default.
The color system is designed to support optimized contrast in color combinations.

accessibility_and_compliance.positioning: Accessibility is an embedded BDDS concern, not an optional checklist applied at the end of a project.

core_expectations: Use accessible color combinations and sufficient contrast.
Use readable typography and scalable text behavior.
Avoid relying on text embedded in images without alternatives.
Provide alt text and ARIA labels where needed.
Support logical keyboard focus and navigation.
Use captions or alternatives for audiovisual content.
Maintain accessible interaction states such as hover, focus, disabled, and error states.

The move toward a headless design system increases compatibility with automation.
